script.opening: (Worried, tired; Leo is on her lap, pale and grizzly.) "Doctor, I'm probably overreacting, but Leo's come up in these little red spots all over his legs, and he's got bruises I can't explain — he hasn't banged himself. He's gone really pale, he's shattered all the time, off his food, and he's just not himself. He's had a couple of temperatures too. My mum says it's probably just a virus going round nursery — is it? I couldn't settle until I'd spoken to someone."

facts.text: Tiny red-purple dots on both legs and his tummy, more over the last few days. If asked to do the glass test: "No… they're still there. They don't fade." Will show them on camera. Not spreading fast today.
Bruises on his shins, back and one on his tummy, appearing over two weeks. "He hasn't banged himself — I'd know, he's not been running about." No nosebleeds, bleeding gums or blood in his wee or poo.

"He's awake — he's here on my lap, just clingy and grizzly." Pale. Doesn't feel hot right now; last temperature 38.1°C two nights ago, settled with paracetamol. If asked: no neck stiffness, not bothered by light, no fits, not floppy, breathing normally, hands and feet warm. Responds to her and watches the screen.
"Gradually. Over about two weeks." Very tired, naps a lot more. "Off his food. He's drinking a bit" — wet nappies/wees about four today. Two low temperatures. Lost a little weight — trousers loose.

"He hasn't said anything about pain, he's just miserable." If asked: doesn't want to walk much and wants to be carried, cried when she lifted him under the arms. She thinks she felt lumps in his neck. Tummy looks a bit bigger.
Born at term, healthy, all immunisations up to date including MenB. No medicines (paracetamol only), no allergies. No recent new medicines. Goes to nursery three days a week; a few colds going round.
Lives with Hayley (28, works in a café) and her partner, Leo's dad, Jamie. No family history of bleeding problems or blood disorders. No social worker involvement. Mum can drive and has a car.

Anxious and apologetic. Volunteer the spots, bruises, pallor and tiredness; give the other details when asked. Keep saying "Everyone keeps saying virus. But he's not right." If the doctor dismisses it, push back once: "But he's never been like this." If told he needs to be seen at hospital today, be shocked ("Today? Right now?") then practical: "Yes, I can get him there now."

ice.ideas: "My mum says it's a virus from nursery — maybe it is."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she has been lying awake and has googled bruising and spots; she is frightened it is something serious like leukaemia but scared of being told she's overreacting. "Everyone keeps saying virus. But he's not right."
ice.expectations: "To know whether it's serious — and for someone to take it seriously."

cues: "I'm probably overreacting." — wants her instinct validated.
"He's just not himself." — a parent's strongest warning sign.
"You mean leukaemia?" — if the doctor mentions blood tests or the blood count.

checkpoints.text: SAFETY FIRST: recognises a non-blanching rash in a child and actively excludes MENINGOCOCCAL SEPSIS — assesses fever, toxic appearance, irritability/drowsiness, neck stiffness, perfusion/obs, glass test (the parent can do this on camera; obs and examination need a same-day face-to-face assessment) — and would arrange EMERGENCY (999) admission if febrile/unwell with a non-blanching rash, ahead of any cancer work-up
Knows the NICE NG12 trigger that unexplained PETECHIAE (or hepatosplenomegaly) requires IMMEDIATE specialist assessment for leukaemia — not watchful waiting or "review in a few days"

Identifies the constellation (pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, unexplained bruising/bleeding, generalised lymphadenopathy, bone pain) warranting a VERY URGENT FBC (within 48 hours) to assess for leukaemia

EXAMINES fully and systematically: pallor, rash distribution/blanching, bruising pattern, lymphadenopathy, HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY, bone/joint tenderness, infection signs, and overall illness (NICE NG143 traffic-light system) — face to face, because the rash, nodes, liver and spleen cannot be examined on video

Considers the differential (leukaemia, ITP, HSP, meningococcal sepsis) and keeps SAFEGUARDING/non-accidental injury in mind for unexplained bruising — without prematurely assuming either a benign or a sinister non-cancer cause
VALIDATES the mother’s instinct (a child who is "not himself" is a powerful safety signal), explicitly does not dismiss her as overreacting, and counters the "just a virus" message compassionately

Communicates a serious, urgent plan to a frightened parent clearly and kindly — honest about the need for urgent tests/assessment without catastrophising or falsely reassuring, and checks her understanding and support

Safety-nets robustly: explicit meningococcal/sepsis red flags and 999 advice, the immediate referral/very-urgent FBC arranged with clear timing, who to contact and how, ensures transport/attendance, documents, and follows up — sepsis excluded first, then immediate leukaemia pathway, never reassurance as a viral rash

worked.txt: "You are absolutely not overreacting — you know Leo, and you’ve noticed he’s not himself, and that instinct is exactly what I want to hear about. You did the right thing bringing him in straight away. I can see him on the screen, but I can’t examine him properly on video, so let me check a couple of things with you now and then get him seen in person today."

"First I need to check a few urgent things. These little spots — can you press the side of a clear glass firmly against them and hold it up to the camera: do they fade? … And his temperature, how alert he is, his breathing and colour. I’m making sure there’s nothing that needs a hospital this very minute."

"He needs someone to feel his tummy for his liver and spleen, check the glands in his neck, armpits and groin, look at his colour and the bruises, and see how he is in himself — that has to be done in person, today, and I’m arranging it now. Bear with me — I’m being careful on purpose."

"I want to be straight with you, calmly. These spots — little ones that don’t fade — together with him being pale, tired and off-colour, are things we never sit on in a child. They can have several causes, including something with the blood cells that we must rule out urgently. I’m not saying that’s what it is — but we get it checked today, not in a few days."

"So here’s what I’m doing now: because of these spots I’m arranging for Leo to be seen by the children’s specialists urgently, with an urgent blood count, today. I’ll organise that straight away and tell you exactly where to go and what to expect."

"While we sort this, if Leo becomes drowsy or floppy, the rash spreads quickly, he gets a high fever, cold hands and feet, or you’re frightened by any change — call 999 and say there’s a child with a rash that doesn’t fade. Trust yourself. You’ve done everything right, and I’m going to stay with you through this."

f.learning: A non-blanching (petechial/purpuric) rash in a child is a SAFETY-FIRST presentation: actively exclude MENINGOCOCCAL SEPSIS/meningitis (fever, toxic/ill appearance, irritability or drowsiness, neck stiffness, poor perfusion, rapidly spreading or purpuric rash) — a febrile, unwell child with a non-blanching rash needs EMERGENCY (999) admission, which takes precedence over any cancer work-up. Once acute sepsis is excluded, the NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) children & young people pathway governs: unexplained PETECHIAE or HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY require IMMEDIATE specialist assessment for leukaemia, and a constellation of pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, unexplained persistent infection, generalised lymphadenopathy, persistent/unexplained bone pain, unexplained bruising or bleeding warrants a VERY URGENT FBC (within 48 hours) — in practice, petechiae plus systemic features usually means same-day assessment. Examine fully (pallor, rash blanching/distribution, bruising pattern, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, bone tenderness, NICE NG143 traffic-light system — in person, as video cannot do this), hold the differential (leukaemia, ITP, HSP, meningococcal sepsis) and keep safeguarding/non-accidental injury in mind for unexplained bruising without assuming. The communication core is a frightened, exhausted mother told by family it is "just a virus" yet who knows her child is "not himself": validate that instinct as a powerful safety signal, do not dismiss her, and bring her through a serious, urgent plan honestly and kindly. Safety-net robustly (meningococcal red flags + 999, clear referral timing and contacts) and follow up — sepsis excluded first, then the immediate leukaemia pathway, never reassurance as a viral rash.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG143 (fever in under 5s) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG254 (sepsis, under 16s) · NICE NG240 (meningitis and meningococcal disease, 2024) · NICE CG89 (child maltreatment)
knowledge.summary: A child with a non-blanching rash is seen face to face today. Exclude meningococcal disease first; unexplained petechiae then mean immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia.

points.t: A non-blanching rash is a red feature in NICE NG143. With fever or any sign of being unwell (drowsy, floppy, mottled, cold hands and feet, fast breathing, rapidly spreading rash), treat as possible meningococcal disease or sepsis: emergency transfer by 999 (NICE NG240, NICE NG254). Give parenteral antibiotics before transfer only as NICE NG240 directs; dose per BNFC.

NICE NG12: refer children and young people for immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia if they have unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly. Leo’s petechiae alone meet this — same day, not a routine review.

NICE NG12: offer a very urgent FBC (within 48 hours) for children and young people with pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, unexplained persistent infection, generalised lymphadenopathy, persistent or unexplained bone pain, unexplained bruising or unexplained bleeding. He has several; with petechiae, the paediatric team does this today.
The rash, nodes, liver and spleen cannot be examined on a screen. Ask the parent to do the glass test on camera and look at the child, then arrange same-day face-to-face paediatric assessment.

Leukaemia, immune thrombocytopenia (often a well child with bruising and petechiae), IgA vasculitis (palpable purpura on legs and buttocks), meningococcal disease, other infections, and non-accidental injury. The FBC and film separate most of these.

NICE CG89: consider maltreatment when bruising is unexplained or doesn’t fit the history or the child’s mobility. Here a medical cause is likely and must be investigated first; record the bruise pattern and keep an open mind.

dg.d: Open question to the mother; let her give the whole story including “am I overreacting?”.
Nursery, family advice that it is a virus, her exhaustion, who can support her today.
Glass test on camera; observation; same-day face-to-face paediatric examination including nodes, liver and spleen; FBC and film.
Meningococcal disease, leukaemia, ITP, IgA vasculitis, infection, non-accidental injury — without fixing early.
Screened fever, drowsiness, perfusion, breathing and rash spread first; defined when to call 999.
Unexplained non-blanching petechiae with pallor, fatigue, fever and bruising: NICE NG12 trigger for immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Direct call to the paediatric assessment unit, seen today, transport confirmed, ambulance if any deterioration.
Bruise pattern recorded and safeguarding kept in mind without accusation; mother’s support arranged.
Named 999 symptoms, written handover, GP call the next day.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “not himself” and “bruises I can’t explain” and acted on both.
Idea (virus, per grandmother), concern (something serious; being seen as overreacting), expectation (to know if it is serious).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — she has been lying awake and has googled bruising and spots; she is frightened it is something serious like leukaemia but scared of being told she's overreacting. "Everyone keeps saying virus. But he's not right." — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Hughes. You must be Hayley, and this is Leo. Tell me what’s been happening.

I’m probably overreacting, but he’s got these little red spots all over his legs, and bruises I can’t explain — he hasn’t banged himself. He’s so pale, shattered, off his food, not himself. He’s had a couple of temperatures. My mum says it’s just a virus from nursery. Is it?
You’re not overreacting — you know Leo best, and ‘not himself’ is one of the most important things a parent can tell me. I’m going to check a few urgent things first, then explain what I think. Okay?
model.why: Validates her instinct; sets a safety-first agenda

model.text: Okay.
Have you got a clear glass? Press it firmly on some of the spots and hold the camera close. Do they fade under the glass?
No… they’re still there. They don’t fade.
Thank you. Right now, is he hot? Is he drowsy or floppy, hard to wake, or are his hands and feet cold? Is he breathing fast?
model.why: Screens for meningococcal disease and sepsis

model.text: He’s awake — he’s here on my lap, just clingy and grizzly. He’s pale. He doesn’t feel hot right now.
Are the spots spreading quickly today, or have they come up gradually over the last couple of weeks?
model.why: Separates acute purpura from a subacute picture

model.text: Gradually. Over about two weeks. And the bruises too.
Where are the bruises? And has he had any nosebleeds or bleeding gums, or complained of his legs or bones hurting?
model.why: Bleeding, bruise distribution and bone pain

model.text: On his legs and his tummy. He hasn’t said anything about pain, he’s just miserable.
Has he been eating and drinking, and passing wee?
Off his food. He’s drinking a bit.
What’s been going through your mind while you’ve been watching this?
Everyone keeps saying virus. But he’s not right. I’ve been lying awake. I couldn’t settle until I’d asked someone.
Thank you. Your instinct brought him here, and it was the right call.
model.why: Affirms the mother and counters the dismissal

model.text: I’m going to be honest and calm with you. Spots that don’t fade under a glass, with bruises, paleness and tiredness, are something we never wait on in a child. I don’t think this is just a virus.
What do you think it is?

There are several possibilities. Sometimes the body uses up its clotting cells after an infection, which often gets better by itself. But it can also be a problem with how the blood cells are made, and we must check that today with a blood test and a specialist examination.
model.why: Explains the differential including leukaemia without the word forced on her

model.text: You mean leukaemia?
That’s one of the things the children’s doctors will want to rule out, yes. I’m not saying that’s what it is. But that’s why he needs to be seen today, not in a few days.
model.why: Answers her direct question honestly without catastrophising

model.text: Here’s the plan. I’m ringing the children’s assessment unit at the hospital now to say Leo needs to be seen straight away. They’ll examine him fully, check his glands, tummy, liver and spleen, and do a blood count today.
model.why: Immediate specialist assessment per NICE NG12, with the FBC

model.text: Today? Right now?
Yes, now. Can you get him there straight away? If there’s any difficulty, or if at any point he seems worse, we’ll send an ambulance instead.
Yes, I can get him there now.
Is there someone who can be with you, or look after anything at home?
I’ll ring my mum.

On the way, or at any point: if he becomes drowsy or floppy, the spots spread quickly, he gets a high temperature, cold hands and feet, or you’re frightened by any change — call 999 and say he has a rash that doesn’t fade.
model.why: Explicit meningococcal red flags and 999 route

model.text: So I know I’ve explained it clearly — what are you going to do when we finish?
Take him straight to the children’s unit. They’re expecting us. If he gets floppy or the spots spread, 999.
Exactly. I’ll send them my notes now, and I’ll ring you tomorrow to see how he’s getting on. You’ve done everything right.

social.t: An exhausted mother told by family she is overreacting may doubt herself. Validation keeps her engaged and makes her safety-netting reliable.
Nursery can be told he is unwell and being assessed; no exclusion decision is needed until a diagnosis is known.

legal.t: NICE CG89: unexplained bruising in a young child prompts consideration of maltreatment, alongside medical causes. Record the pattern and the history; if concerns remain after medical assessment, follow local safeguarding procedures.
His mother gives consent for examination and tests. Explain what will happen and why.

professional.t: Know when video is not enough. A child with a non-blanching rash must be seen in person the same day; document why and how you arranged it.
Speak directly to the paediatric team and send a written summary so nothing is lost at the front door.

community.t: If a blood disorder is found, the paediatric team links families to specialist nurses and charities such as Young Lives vs Cancer or ITP Support Association as relevant.

redFlags: Non-blanching rash with fever or an unwell child — possible meningococcal disease, 999
Unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly — immediate specialist assessment (NICE NG12)
Pallor, fatigue, fever, bruising, bleeding, bone pain, generalised lymphadenopathy
psychosocial: Mother exhausted, doubting herself after family said it’s a virus
ice: Idea: “My mum says it’s just a virus from nursery”
Concern: something is seriously wrong; being seen as overreacting
Expectation: to be told whether it is serious

playbook.diagnosis: A 3-year-old with two weeks of non-blanching petechiae, unexplained bruising, pallor, fatigue and intermittent fever. No features of acute meningococcal disease on video, but he needs same-day face-to-face assessment. Unexplained petechiae meet the NICE NG12 criterion for immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia; ITP and other causes are also possible.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “These little spots that don’t fade under a glass, with the bruises and him being pale and tired, mean his blood needs checking today. There are a few possible causes, some that settle on their own, and one we must rule out is a problem with how blood cells are made.”

management.reflectIce: “Everyone’s been telling you it’s a virus, but you knew he wasn’t right. You were right to bring him — and that’s exactly why I want him seen today.”
management.psychosocial: Confirm transport and someone to support her; keep language calm and honest; follow up personally.
sharedPlan: Phone the paediatric assessment unit now: immediate specialist assessment
FBC and film today at the hospital
Ambulance instead if any deterioration or transport problem
safetyNet: Drowsy, floppy, spreading spots, high fever, cold hands and feet — 999, say “rash that doesn’t fade”
Written handover to the paediatric team
GP phone call the next day

pitfalls.intro: This station tests two things in order: exclude meningococcal disease, then act on unexplained petechiae. Communication with a frightened, dismissed mother is the second half of the marks.

items.fail: Labelling it a viral rash and reviewing in a few days.
items.why: NICE NG12: unexplained petechiae in a child mean immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia.
items.fix: Same-day paediatric assessment, arranged by you, today.

items.fail: Going straight to the leukaemia discussion without screening for sepsis or meningococcal disease.
items.why: A non-blanching rash is a NICE NG143 red feature; the acute emergency must be excluded first.
items.fix: Glass test, fever, drowsiness, perfusion, breathing and rash spread in the first minutes.

items.fail: Trying to finish the assessment on video, or booking a routine face-to-face appointment.
items.why: Nodes, liver, spleen and the rash cannot be examined on a screen, and the timeframe is immediate.
items.fix: Use video for the glass test and observation, then phone the paediatric unit.

items.fail: Agreeing she might be overreacting, or ignoring the family’s “it’s a virus”.
items.why: Dismissing parental concern loses Relating marks and weakens her safety-netting.
items.fix: “You’re not overreacting — ‘not himself’ is one of the most important things you can tell me.”

items.fail: Dodging “Is it leukaemia?” or answering with alarm.
items.why: Evasion erodes trust; blunt confirmation of an unproven diagnosis is also wrong.
items.fix: “That’s one thing they’ll want to rule out. I’m not saying it is. That’s why today.”

items.fail: Vague safety-netting — “go to A&E if worried”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-nets are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Named signs, the 999 route and the phrase “rash that doesn’t fade”, plus teach-back.

timeMap.d: Let her finish, then say plainly she is not overreacting.
Glass test on camera; fever, drowsiness, perfusion, breathing, rash spread; bleeding and bone pain; feeding.
Her fear and the family telling her it is a virus.
Not a virus; possibilities including a blood problem; ring the paediatric unit now; transport; support.
999 symptoms, teach-back, handover, GP follow-up call.

wordPics.fail: Calls it a viral rash and reviews in a few days; or tries to manage entirely over video; or frightens the mother with “this could be leukaemia or meningitis” and no clear plan.
wordPics.pass: Does the glass test, screens for sepsis, recognises unexplained petechiae as an NICE NG12 immediate-referral trigger, arranges same-day paediatric assessment and gives 999 advice.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: validates the mother first; answers “leukaemia?” honestly and calmly; confirms transport and support; holds the differential including safeguarding without accusation; teach-back and a next-day call.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably a virus — let’s see him again if it’s not better in a few days.”
avoid.instead: “Spots that don’t fade under a glass in a child who isn’t himself need to be seen today.”
avoid.why: Unexplained petechiae in a child are an NICE NG12 trigger for immediate specialist assessment.

avoid.dont: “How did he get these bruises?” (asked flatly, as an accusation)
avoid.instead: “Where are the bruises, and has he had any bleeding from his nose or gums?”
avoid.why: Gather the pattern clinically; safeguarding stays in mind without alienating a frightened parent.

avoid.instead: “It could be a problem with how the blood cells are made, which we must check today — I’m not saying that’s what it is.”
avoid.why: Honest without delivering a diagnosis you do not have.

Exactly. I’ll send them my notes now, and I’ll ring you tomorrow to see how he’s getting on. You’ve done everything right.

SCA_STEM.name: Leo Whitfield
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations. Video appointment booked by mother today: “spots and bruises, not himself”.
SCA_STEM.reason: About 2 weeks of small red-purple spots, unexplained bruises, pallor, tiredness and a couple of temperatures.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG143 (fever in under 5s) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · NICE NG254 (sepsis, under 16s) · NICE NG240 (meningitis and meningococcal disease, 2024) · NICE CG89 (child maltreatment)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A child with a non-blanching rash is seen face to face today. Exclude meningococcal disease first; unexplained petechiae then mean immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia.

points.t: A non-blanching rash is a red feature in NICE NG143. With fever or any sign of being unwell (drowsy, floppy, mottled, cold hands and feet, fast breathing, rapidly spreading rash), treat as possible meningococcal disease or sepsis: emergency transfer by 999 (NICE NG240, NICE NG254). Give parenteral antibiotics before transfer only as NICE NG240 directs; dose per BNFC.

NICE NG12: refer children and young people for immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia if they have unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly. Leo’s petechiae alone meet this — same day, not a routine review.

NICE NG12: offer a very urgent FBC (within 48 hours) for children and young people with pallor, persistent fatigue, unexplained fever, unexplained persistent infection, generalised lymphadenopathy, persistent or unexplained bone pain, unexplained bruising or unexplained bleeding. He has several; with petechiae, the paediatric team does this today.
The rash, nodes, liver and spleen cannot be examined on a screen. Ask the parent to do the glass test on camera and look at the child, then arrange same-day face-to-face paediatric assessment.

Leukaemia, immune thrombocytopenia (often a well child with bruising and petechiae), IgA vasculitis (palpable purpura on legs and buttocks), meningococcal disease, other infections, and non-accidental injury. The FBC and film separate most of these.

NICE CG89: consider maltreatment when bruising is unexplained or doesn’t fit the history or the child’s mobility. Here a medical cause is likely and must be investigated first; record the bruise pattern and keep an open mind.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question to the mother; let her give the whole story including “am I overreacting?”.
Nursery, family advice that it is a virus, her exhaustion, who can support her today.
Picked up “not himself” and “bruises I can’t explain” and acted on both.
Idea (virus, per grandmother), concern (something serious; being seen as overreacting), expectation (to know if it is serious).
Glass test on camera; observation; same-day face-to-face paediatric examination including nodes, liver and spleen; FBC and film.
Meningococcal disease, leukaemia, ITP, IgA vasculitis, infection, non-accidental injury — without fixing early.
Screened fever, drowsiness, perfusion, breathing and rash spread first; defined when to call 999.
Unexplained non-blanching petechiae with pallor, fatigue, fever and bruising: NICE NG12 trigger for immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia.
Direct call to the paediatric assessment unit, seen today, transport confirmed, ambulance if any deterioration.
Bruise pattern recorded and safeguarding kept in mind without accusation; mother’s support arranged.
Named 999 symptoms, written handover, GP call the next day.

social.t: An exhausted mother told by family she is overreacting may doubt herself. Validation keeps her engaged and makes her safety-netting reliable.
Nursery can be told he is unwell and being assessed; no exclusion decision is needed until a diagnosis is known.

legal.t: NICE CG89: unexplained bruising in a young child prompts consideration of maltreatment, alongside medical causes. Record the pattern and the history; if concerns remain after medical assessment, follow local safeguarding procedures.
His mother gives consent for examination and tests. Explain what will happen and why.

professional.t: Know when video is not enough. A child with a non-blanching rash must be seen in person the same day; document why and how you arranged it.
Speak directly to the paediatric team and send a written summary so nothing is lost at the front door.

community.t: If a blood disorder is found, the paediatric team links families to specialist nurses and charities such as Young Lives vs Cancer or ITP Support Association as relevant.

redFlags: Non-blanching rash with fever or an unwell child — possible meningococcal disease, 999
Unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly — immediate specialist assessment (NICE NG12)
Pallor, fatigue, fever, bruising, bleeding, bone pain, generalised lymphadenopathy
psychosocial: Mother exhausted, doubting herself after family said it’s a virus
ice: Idea: “My mum says it’s just a virus from nursery”
Concern: something is seriously wrong; being seen as overreacting
Expectation: to be told whether it is serious

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: A 3-year-old with two weeks of non-blanching petechiae, unexplained bruising, pallor, fatigue and intermittent fever. No features of acute meningococcal disease on video, but he needs same-day face-to-face assessment. Unexplained petechiae meet the NICE NG12 criterion for immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia; ITP and other causes are also possible.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “These little spots that don’t fade under a glass, with the bruises and him being pale and tired, mean his blood needs checking today. There are a few possible causes, some that settle on their own, and one we must rule out is a problem with how blood cells are made.”

management.reflectIce: “Everyone’s been telling you it’s a virus, but you knew he wasn’t right. You were right to bring him — and that’s exactly why I want him seen today.”
management.psychosocial: Confirm transport and someone to support her; keep language calm and honest; follow up personally.
sharedPlan: Phone the paediatric assessment unit now: immediate specialist assessment
FBC and film today at the hospital
Ambulance instead if any deterioration or transport problem
safetyNet: Drowsy, floppy, spreading spots, high fever, cold hands and feet — 999, say “rash that doesn’t fade”
Written handover to the paediatric team
GP phone call the next day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests two things in order: exclude meningococcal disease, then act on unexplained petechiae. Communication with a frightened, dismissed mother is the second half of the marks.

items.fail: Labelling it a viral rash and reviewing in a few days.
items.why: NICE NG12: unexplained petechiae in a child mean immediate specialist assessment for leukaemia.
items.fix: Same-day paediatric assessment, arranged by you, today.

items.fail: Going straight to the leukaemia discussion without screening for sepsis or meningococcal disease.
items.why: A non-blanching rash is a NICE NG143 red feature; the acute emergency must be excluded first.
items.fix: Glass test, fever, drowsiness, perfusion, breathing and rash spread in the first minutes.

items.fail: Trying to finish the assessment on video, or booking a routine face-to-face appointment.
items.why: Nodes, liver, spleen and the rash cannot be examined on a screen, and the timeframe is immediate.
items.fix: Use video for the glass test and observation, then phone the paediatric unit.

items.fail: Agreeing she might be overreacting, or ignoring the family’s “it’s a virus”.
items.why: Dismissing parental concern loses Relating marks and weakens her safety-netting.
items.fix: “You’re not overreacting — ‘not himself’ is one of the most important things you can tell me.”

items.fail: Dodging “Is it leukaemia?” or answering with alarm.
items.why: Evasion erodes trust; blunt confirmation of an unproven diagnosis is also wrong.
items.fix: “That’s one thing they’ll want to rule out. I’m not saying it is. That’s why today.”

items.fail: Vague safety-netting — “go to A&E if worried”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-nets are standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Named signs, the 999 route and the phrase “rash that doesn’t fade”, plus teach-back.
